diagnosis: Three rollouts (0, 1, 2) settled and two passed (1, 2); rollout 0 failed on content check C4 (attendance_action); rollout 3 auto-failed on the turn cap at 18 turns without ever settling, having revealed PF3, PF1, PF2 (PF1 twice) but never PF4 (A5 never disclosed the guardian's check-in information). CHECK C4 in rollout 0 (ENCODING MISMATCH): A4 revealed PF3 at turn 9, stating 'all absence dates in this episode qualify for the MED excused-attendance code and require no attendance intervention or truancy referral,' and the settlement's attendance_action field reads 'All absence dates in this episode coded as MED-excused; no attendance intervention or truancy referral required' — this is a faithful use of PF3. The check C4 still returned false despite the value being substantively correct. The passing rollouts (1 and 2) used the phrasing 'MED excused' (space, no hyphen) in their attendance_action fields and C4 passed there. The failing rollout used 'MED-excused' (hyphenated), which is the one phrasings difference between pass and fail on C4 across the otherwise-identical content. This is an ENCODING MISMATCH: the check appears to require the non-hyphenated form 'MED excused' but the model naturally wrote 'MED-excused.' TURN-CAP AUTO-FAIL in rollout 3 (STRUCTURAL problem, not pacing): The conversation ran 18 turns and consumed the entire cap without A1 ever issuing a settle action, even though PF1, PF2, and PF3 were all revealed by turn 14. Two turns were wasted on unparsable model outputs (turns 1 and 5, both A2 and A3 respectively), which disrupted the normal speaking order and caused A1 to spend turns 6–16 re-establishing the turn order and repeatedly asking each agent to share. A5 (Ms. Okafor) was repeatedly told to wait until after Nurse Rivera and Ms. Brooks, and by the time A1 explicitly invited A5 at turn 16, the cap was exhausted before A5 could reveal PF4 or before A1 could settle. The root cause is that the unparsable outputs broke the round-robin sequencing and caused excessive orchestration overhead, not that 18 turns was inherently insufficient for 5 agents — rollouts 1 and 2 settled cleanly in 10–12 turns. Increasing the turn cap alone would not reliably fix this because the broken turns caused cascading re-coordination overhead; the structural fix is to ensure the settle-eligibility condition does not require strict sequential completion of all agents before settling can occur, or to add error-recovery handling so a single unparsable turn does not derail the entire round-robin order.
